analysis.one_liner: Requires phone companies to get written customer consent before switching long-distance service.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required written consent before a phone company could switch someone's long-distance carrier, died in a House subcommittee with 29 bipartisan cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: "Slamming" is when a phone company switches your long-distance carrier without your permission and bills you at worse rates. This bill would have required a signed, standalone written form before any switch, made the slamming carrier pay back your switching fees and up to six months of long-distance charges, set up state-run complaint systems with the FCC as a backstop, and fined carriers whose unauthorized-switch rates exceeded federal limits. It never advanced past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of household and small-business telephone customers of the era who were vulnerable to having their long-distance carrier switched without their consent. They would gain the right to written proof before any switch, an easy complaint channel listed on their phone bill, and reimbursement of switching fees and up to six months of charges from any carrier that slammed them. State utility commissions would also gain a defined role policing the problem.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a carrier to have a written, signed, dated change authorization from the customer before switching the customer's interstate long-distance provider — and bars the authorization from being buried in another document, bundled with a bill, or tied to a promotional offer
Makes a carrier that slams a customer liable for the switching fees and for all interstate long-distance charges the customer incurred, for up to six months after the unauthorized switch

Sets up a slamming complaint system in every state — run by the state utility commission if it certifies one, otherwise by the FCC — that records complaints, rules on violations, and tracks how many unauthorized switches each carrier commits each month
Requires every long-distance bill to tell customers how to file a slamming complaint, including a phone number to call
Directs the FCC to study slamming rates and set maximum acceptable rates of unauthorized switches, with carriers that exceed the limit subject to federal forfeiture penalties

analysis.who_pays: Long-distance carriers and their sales agents. Carriers that slammed would owe customers their switching fees and up to six months of long-distance charges, plus FCC forfeiture penalties if their unauthorized-switch rate exceeded the federal limit. Even compliant carriers would bear the cost of using a standardized written authorization form, keeping duplicate copies for customers, and printing complaint information on every bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Long-distance carriers and their sales agents

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces the existing interstate slamming liability rule rather than simply adding to it: it rewrites the old provision so it applies only to intrastate changes, so customers' protections would depend entirely on the new complaint-and-penalty system working as designed

Enforcement would be slow to arrive — the bill takes effect only 12 months after enactment, and the forfeiture penalties do not apply until the FCC completes a study and sets performance limits, adding at least another year

Legitimate carriers would face real compliance costs: producing an FCC-approved standard authorization form, providing duplicate copies customers keep, and adding complaint notices to every monthly bill
The per-customer remedy is capped — reimbursement of switching fees and up to six months of long-distance charges — which may not fully make a customer whole in every case

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and directly aimed at a widespread practice that cost ordinary households money on their phone bills. The main costs fall on the industry being policed, which is the point of the bill, though the delay before penalties take effect and the replacement of the existing liability rule are design choices an honest supporter would acknowledge. On balance the benefits to telephone customers outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to a House subcommittee two weeks after introduction and sat there, with no hearing or vote, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on July 9, 1997, joined by six original cosponsors from both parties
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over telecommunications
On July 18, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection — the last action ever taken on the bill
Twenty-nine members cosponsored the bill — 23 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but it never received a hearing, a subcommittee vote, or a floor vote
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill still stuck in subcommittee and every provision expiring

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Long-distance carriers and their marketing agents came out ahead: the existing rules they operated under stayed in place, and they never faced the written-consent requirement, per-customer liability, or per-carrier penalty limits the bill would have imposed. Customers who were slammed kept whatever remedies state law and the weaker existing federal rule provided.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split is unknown; sponsorship was bipartisan, with 23 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent among the 29 cosponsors.

industries.note: Carriers gained customers and revenue through unauthorized switches, and the slamming carrier kept the difference between rates. The bill would have ended that practice, forced refunds of fees and up to six months of charges, and exposed high-slamming carriers to federal fines.

industries.industry: Telecom sales agents and telemarketing firms
industries.note: Third-party agents earned commissions for switching customers, often using loosely documented sign-ups. The bill's written-authorization rules — standalone forms, no bundling with bills or promotions, duplicate copies — would have shut down those sales tactics.

States could certify to run the slamming complaint system for interstate service in their state, with records of violations and monthly per-carrier counts reported to the FCC. The bill explicitly preserves states' ability to add their own consumer protections.
